claims.claim: The two source-stated bounds imply total update time Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). This meets Õ(n√m) when m≤n^(6/5) and when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n; over all m it is within an Õ(n^(1/4)) factor of the target.
claims.evidence: For the sparse bound, m^(4/3)≤n√m is equivalent to m^(5/6)≤n, hence m≤n^(6/5). For the dense bound, n²/(n√m)=n/√m is polylogarithmic when m≥n²/polylog(n). The ratio min{n²,m^(4/3)}/(n√m)=min{n/√m,m^(5/6)/n}; its increasing and decreasing branches meet at m=n^(3/2), where the ratio is n^(1/4).
claims.witness: The crossover m=n^(3/2) makes both available bounds n² and realizes the claimed worst-case n^(1/4) ratio.
claims.search_method: Symbolic exponent comparison followed by exact-integer inequality checks.

claims.claim: Balanced-cut lemma: for every order-violating insertion u→v into a DAG, either the insertion closes a cycle, or one can find equally sized sets B,F and a cut c such that F consists of the descendants of v at or left of c, B consists of the ancestors of u right of c, and the stable order (L\F),B,F,(R\B) is topological. In the latter case, all |B||F| ordered pairs in B×F become newly reachable.
claims.evidence: If v reaches u, u→v closes a cycle. Otherwise the inclusive descendant and ancestor sets D,C inside [v,u] are disjoint. During a cut sweep, |D∩L|−|C∩R| starts negative, ends positive, and changes only by unit positive steps, so it attains zero with v∈F and u∈B. The only newly reversed old-edge categories are F→L\F, R\B→B, and F→B; these contradict descendant closure, ancestor closure, and absence of a v-to-u path, respectively. The new edge points B→F. Every b∈B reaches every f∈F through b→u→v→f, while the old topological order placed f before b, proving every such pair is fresh.
claims.witness: The zero of the integer cut-sweep supplies the required B,F,c constructively.
claims.search_method: Direct invariant proof plus exhaustive enumeration of all fixed-order DAGs through six vertices and every candidate violating insertion.

claims.claim: The balanced-cut construction gives an explicit combinatorial algorithm with total time Õ(m+n√m+A), where A is the total number of adjacency entries scanned from selected forward vertices and selected backward vertices. Consequently it attains Õ(n√m) whenever A=Õ(n√m), including sequences in which every selected forward vertex has polylogarithmic out-degree and every selected backward vertex has polylogarithmic in-degree at its expansion time.
claims.evidence: For each acyclic violating update, q² ordered pairs become newly reachable. Monotonicity makes these charged pairs disjoint across updates, so Σq_i²≤n(n−1); Cauchy–Schwarz gives Σq_i=O(n√m). Heap operations generated by scanned edges cost Õ(A), selected-vertex and stable-order operations cost Õ(Σq_i), and input/root work costs Õ(m); the sole terminal cycle search adds at most Õ(n)+its A contribution. Thus the stated total follows. Under the directional polylog-degree condition, A=Õ(Σq_i+n), and for a simple graph m≤n² implies m≤n√m.
claims.witness: The accounting identity Σq_i≤√(mΣq_i²)≤n√m is supported by the fresh-pair invariant from claim 1.
claims.search_method: Independent amortized-analysis reconstruction; exhaustive tests also confirmed that the paired compatible search returns balanced fresh-pair sets.

claims.claim: Full adjacency-list rescanning cannot be charged automatically to the balanced-search vertex bound: there is a DAG sequence with n=2r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, yet rescanning the selected forward list costs r².
claims.evidence: With order v,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r, the 3r initial edges v→w_j, z→w_j, and u_i→z are consistent. Before inserting u_i→v, the relevant descendant and ancestor sets are {v} and {u_i}, so q=1. Vertex u_i already reaches z and every w_j and has no proper ancestor, hence only (u_i,v) is newly reachable. Vertex v nevertheless has r outgoing entries on each of r violating updates, producing exactly r² full-list scans. Counts are n=2r+2 and m=4r.
claims.witness: The construction works for every integer r≥1; the checker reconstructs every update and its exact reachability delta for 1≤r≤40.
claims.search_method: Exact construction simulation with integer reachability closure and stable reorder checks.

claims.claim: Interval-pruning lemma: in a compatible-search round whose current forward-minimum and backward-maximum candidates are f≺b, forward expansion may ignore out-neighbors right of b and backward expansion may ignore in-neighbors left of f. The pruned search still detects every cycle-forming insertion and, in the non-cycle branch, selects the same first q descendants and last q ancestors that yield a balanced cut.
claims.evidence: Forward extracted candidates are monotone rightward and backward extracted candidates monotone leftward. Thus a forward neighbor discarded to the right of the current b can never participate in a later compatible pair; its descendants lie still farther right. The backward argument is symmetric, proving preservation of the non-cycle selections. For a cycle path v=p₀→⋯→p_k=u, if expansion of p_i first discards p_(i+1)>b, then every suffix vertex is right of b. Backward expansion from u has already propagated down that suffix: at each earlier expansion its predecessor lay right of the then-current forward frontier and was not pruned. Consequently p_i belongs to both reached sets, forcing cycle detection.
claims.witness: Full and pruned searches produced identical non-cycle selections and identical cycle decisions for all 251,085 tested insertions through n=6.
claims.search_method: Monotone-frontier/path-induction proof plus exhaustive comparison against unpruned compatible search.

claims.claim: Selective-expansion refinement: let H sum, over all compatible-search expansions, min{outdeg(f),|{x:f≺x≼b}|} on the forward side and min{indeg(b),|{x:f≼x≺b}|} on the backward side. There is an explicit combinatorial implementation with total update time Õ(m+n√m+H). Moreover H≤A, and H=O(m) on the rescanning family of the preceding audited claim.
claims.evidence: The algorithm can compare the stored degree with the sequence-tree interval size, then either scan the adjacency list or enumerate the interval and query a deterministic edge dictionary. Its probes and generated candidates equal the chosen minimum up to logarithmic overhead. Claim 4 supplies correctness, while claim 2's remaining accounting is unchanged, giving Õ(m+n√m+H). Each minimum is bounded by the corresponding scanned degree, so H≤A termwise. In claim 3's family, f=v and b=u_i are adjacent, giving forward cost min{r,1}=1 and backward cost min{0,1}=0 per update; hence H=r=O(m).
claims.witness: On the r-update rescanning family, A=r² but the selective parameter is exactly H=r.
claims.search_method: Operation-by-operation cost reconstruction, termwise comparison with A, and exact family simulation.

claims.claim: The selective parameter H is still not bounded by Õ(n√m): there is a DAG sequence with n=3r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, but both the forward degree and active forward interval have size at least r, giving H=r².
claims.evidence: In the order v,x₁,…,x_r,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r with the stated initial edges, before update u_i→v the maintained order is u₁,…,u_(i−1),v,x₁,…,x_r,u_i,… . The balanced sets are {v},{u_i}; u_i already reaches z and all w_j, so only (u_i,v) is fresh. At forward expansion, outdeg(v)=r and (v,u_i] contains r+1 vertices, contributing r. There are r such updates, so H=r², whereas n√m=(3r+2)·2√r=Θ(r^(3/2)).
claims.witness: The exact ratio H/(n√m)=r²/((3r+2)·2√r)=Θ(√r), which is not polylogarithmically bounded.
claims.search_method: Exact update-sequence simulation and asymptotic ratio calculation.

claims.claim: Padding sharpens the selective-expansion obstruction across every subquadratic density: for integers r≥1 and 0≤s≤r, adjoining a disconnected s-vertex transitive DAG to the preceding sequence gives n=3r+s+2, m=4r+binom(s,2), while every violating update still has q=1, creates one new reachability pair, and contributes total H=r². Consequently H/(n√m)=Θ(r/√(r+s²)). For every fixed a∈[1,2), choosing s=⌈r^(a/2)⌉ gives m=Θ(n^a) and a polynomial gap Θ(n^(1−a/2)); at a=3/2 the gap is Θ(n^(1/4)), whereas at the quadratic or polylogarithmically near-quadratic boundary it is only constant or polylogarithmic.
claims.evidence: The disconnected padding adds exactly s vertices and binom(s,2) order-consistent edges and cannot affect searches or reachability in the original component. Since s≤r, n=Θ(r), m=Θ(r+s²), and H=r², yielding the displayed ratio. For fixed 1≤a<2 and s=⌈r^(a/2)⌉, n=Θ(r), m=Θ(r^a), and the ratio is Θ(r^(1−a/2))=Θ(n^(1−a/2)). Setting r=t⁴,s=t³ gives the exact a=3/2 scaling and n^(1/4) gap. Taking s=Θ(r) gives a constant gap; taking s=r/polylog(r) gives a polylogarithmic gap.
claims.witness: The integer parameterization r=t⁴,s=t³ has H=t⁸, n=Θ(t⁴), and m=Θ(t⁶), so H/(n√m)=Θ(t)=Θ(n^(1/4)).
claims.search_method: Exact edge/vertex counting, component-separation reasoning, and integer parameter checks.

target_evidence: The draft proves valid regime comparisons, a balanced-cut compatible-search framework with conditional Õ(m+n√m+A) and Õ(m+n√m+H) bounds, and explicit families showing why its scan parameters can exceed the target. It does not bound A or H by Õ(n√m) in general and expressly supplies no different unconditional combinatorial algorithm. Thus it makes material correct progress but does not prove the entire requested target. Its stated PARTIAL resolution is accurate.
